content: Rosa × damascena, commonly referred to as the Damask rose or simply Damask, is a hybrid rose species that originates from the crossbreeding of Rosa gallica and Rosa moschata. This plant is a deciduous shrub that can grow up to 2.2 meters in height. Its stems are densely covered with stout, curved prickles and stiff bristles. The leaves of this shrub are pinnate in structure, typically consisting of five leaflets, though occasionally there may be seven. The Damask rose holds significant historical and botanical importance as a prominent type of Old Rose. It has also played a crucial role in the lineage of many other rose varieties. Historical accounts attribute the introduction of this rose to Europe to the crusader Robert de Brie, who is believed to have brought it from Persia between the years 1254 and 1276. The name Damask is derived from Damascus, a major city in the region where the rose was historically cultivated. This rose is particularly celebrated for its exquisite fragrance. Its flowers are commercially harvested to produce rose oil, which is a key ingredient in the perfume industry. In perfumery, the scent derived from this rose is often referred to as Damascus rose. Rosa × damascena is classified into two main varieties based on their flowering seasons: 1. Summer Damasks (R × damascena nothovar damascena): These roses have a short flowering period that occurs only during the summer. 2. Autumn Damasks (R × damascena nothovar semperflorens): These roses have an extended flowering season that continues into the autumn. Apart from their longer blooming period, they are otherwise indistinguishable from the Summer Damasks. A well-known example of Rosa × damascena is the Ispahan rose, which remains popular to this day. Additionally, the hybrid Rosa × centifolia is partially derived from Rosa × damascena.
